activities.anchor: The loss function is the contract between you and the algorithm
activities.caption: pair each loss with what it punishes
activities.name: carLossMatch

config.prompt: The contract defines 'wrong' — pair each loss with its temperament:

pairs.right: squaring punishes large misses disproportionately — an error of 10 costs 100× an error of 1
mean absolute error — misses priced linearly
gentle when right and confident; brutal when confidently wrong

config.why: Both losses fall out of maximum-likelihood reasoning: squared error assumes Gaussian noise; log loss takes probability claims seriously.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the naive baseline's RMSE
activities.name: carBaselineEstimate

config.prompt: The eight apartments have mean price $232.5k. Predicting that mean every time — roughly what RMSE does this naive baseline score?
config.why: About $82k — exactly the standard deviation of the prices. Any model that cannot beat $82k is literally worse than ignoring the input.
config.context: The least-squares line reaches RMSE ≈ $11k, roughly a seven-fold improvement, with R² ≈ 0.98.

activities.anchor: Least squares minimises the squared vertical gaps
activities.caption: find the faulty line — how the line is found
activities.name: carLineSpot

config.prompt: This fitting summary contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Least squares minimises the squared vertical gaps between line and points.
The fitted line is price ≈ 132×area + 47 — about $132 per square foot.
Its RMSE is about $11k, roughly a seven-fold improvement over the baseline.
R² = 0.98 means the line explains 98% of the price variance.
The least-squares line is found by chasing whichever single point sits furthest from the line.
config.correction: It is the bottom of a smooth bowl — the least-squares line balances all the vertical gaps at once, not a chase of any single point.
config.why: Drag the fit sliders in the widget: move slope or intercept off the optimum and watch the gaps balloon uniformly — no single point commands the line.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — from score to chance
activities.name: carSigmoidCloze

config.text: For categories, compute a linear score z = w·x + b, then squash it through the %%0%% function, which maps any number into (0, 1) — a %%1%%. A score of 0 becomes %%2%%. Despite 'regression' in its name, logistic regression is a %%3%%.
config.hint: The squishing function, what its output means, where zero lands, and the naming trap.

activities.caption: set the operating point on the probability dial
activities.name: carThresholdPlace

config.prompt: You want only near-certain spam filtered, accepting more spam in your inbox. Where does the threshold sit?
config.why: 0.9 — only near-certain spam gets filtered, at the cost of more spam in your inbox. The model supplies the score; the operating point is a choice that belongs to the business, not the data scientist.
config.context: At 0.5, an email claiming 0.51 spam is already delivered to the junk folder.

activities.anchor: A straight line through the apartment data may be too stiff
activities.caption: file the failure — overfit, underfit or leak?
activities.name: carFlexBuckets

config.prompt: Three ways a flexible model fails — file each symptom:

items.label: a tree deep enough to hit every training point exactly — memorised noise
near-zero training error, poor error on new data
a model too stiff to capture real structure
a straight line through prices that bend near the city centre
a 'sales prediction' model that accidentally learned the week the sale was recorded

config.why: The third failure is the most dangerous in practice — leakage inflates results until the model meets reality.

activities.anchor: A model that outputs scores can be evaluated at every threshold simultaneously
activities.caption: which curve is the better model?
activities.name: carROCTrace

config.prompt: Three ROC curves, one per model. Which belongs to the strong one?
config.why: A useless model traces the diagonal; a strong one hugs the top-left corner. AUC is the probability that a random fraud scores above a random legitimate transaction — 0.9 means it orders them right 9 times in 10.

activities.anchor: One more professional judgement: interpretability scales with stakes
activities.caption: ship the explanation — three compliance routes
activities.name: carExplainBranch

config.root: You are shipping a model that informs regulated decisions — credit, medicine, parole. Explanation is not optional.

choices.label: A random forest, explanations promised later
Linear regression — reasoning in its coefficients
Random forest + SHAP attribution per decision

blackbox.text: A movie recommender can stay a black box; a parole model cannot — regulators require explanation (adverse action notices under US fair-lending law, explanation rights under GDPR).

linear.text: Interpretability scales with stakes: linear regression hands you its reasoning in its coefficients — the weakest learner that still explains itself.

shap.text: SHAP values distribute each prediction's departure from average across its input features — individual-decision explanations for a model that is itself opaque.

config.why: The data scientist ships a calibrated score; the threshold — and the explanation duty — belong to whoever owns the stakes.
